extracted.intended_audience: historians of mathematics, history-of-science scholars, graduate students and researchers preparing or evaluating chapters on early modern mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing or evaluating scholarly chapters on mathematics in Early Modern and Enlightenment Europe, focusing on themes like numeracy, practice and profession, invention, worldviews, technology, and representation. Emphasizes appropriate scope (geography, chronology), sources, methodological constraints, and thematic organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal and geographic grounding
rubrics_metrics.description: Shed light on when (periodization) and where (geographic areas) mathematics became increasingly useful and who did it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish clear chronological boundaries (e.g., fifteenth–seventeenth centuries, long 18th century) and geographic focus (often Western Europe, but situate in broader global contexts where relevant). Identify actors (practitioners, merchants, artisans, learned mathematicians) and trace change over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on numeration systems and calculation methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe the evolution/transformation of different systems of numeration and calculation methods (e.g., counters/calculating boards with Roman numeration vs. written calculation with Indo-Arabic positional decimal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relate methods to material tools and number systems, geographic spread (positional decimal in Southern Europe from 12th century), coexistence of multiple methods (counters, written calculation, finger counting), and technical improvements (printing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Users' needs and heterogeneity of numerical skills
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for heterogeneity of numerical skills across social groups and occupations (shopkeepers, international merchants, urban vs rural populations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate users by needs (accounting sophistication in large Italian cities vs elsewhere), literacy rates, and the social contexts that shaped numeracy uptake; avoid one-size-fits-all narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of textbooks and practical sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Use textbooks and other accessible written sources to study everyday numeracy and the transmission of arithmetic from the fifteenth to seventeenth centuries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat textbooks as primary evidence for practices and users; analyze how texts were used, diversified, and who their audiences were.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interplay between practice and speculative mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine the relationship between practical (manual/technical) mathematics and speculative/intellectual mathematics, avoiding modern applied/abstract dichotomies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize practitioners often 'did mathematics through the exercise of their disciplinary practice' rather than applying a separate independent mathematics. Use examples (astronomy, surveying, navigation, perspective) to show integrated practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional and organisational factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyse how academies, teaching institutions, patronage, guilds, public administration, and mathematical societies shaped mathematical identity and practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider institutional positions (Mathematicus, court appointments), teaching/learning settings (schools, universities, private tuition), patronage networks, and the material culture (books and instruments) that instantiate disciplinary identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of tools, books, and instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat books, instruments and material tools as characteristic and constitutive elements of mathematical activity and identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine how instruments and printed works circulated, how they were used to teach, legitimize, or market mathematical expertise, and how they reflected occupational practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invention versus tradition
rubrics_metrics.description: Balance accounts of invention with continuity from classical (Greek) traditions; show how early modern mathematicians both relied on and supplemented antiquity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss cases where classical methods inspired new methods (e.g., Archimedean influence on quadrature), but also development of analytic/algebraic methods (Descartes) and re-conceptualization of analysis/synthesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem-solving orientation and methodological constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Highlight the early modern emphasis on resolution of mathematical problems (constructibility, straightedge-and-compass questions) and methodological constraints coming from tradition or philosophical prerequisites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how methods were judged (e.g., whether a problem required straightedge-and-compass), include philosophical criteria such as Descartes' clear-and-distinct ideas, and show how such constraints shaped allowable inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textual genres and communication channels
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the diversity of textual forms (printed books, journals, correspondence, manuscripts) through which mathematics was developed and transmitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for the role of scientific journals (Acta Eruditorum), correspondence networks (Mersenne), first printed editions (Euclid 1492), and how publication venues affected reception and invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematics as a touchstone for certainty (worldviews)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine how mathematics served as a model of certitude and influenced philosophical worldviews and methods (e.g., Descartes, Spinoza, Leibniz), while avoiding retrospective, univocal interpretations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze debates about certitudo vs adequatio, the role of mathematics in changing conceptions of truth, and plural meanings of the 'mathematical method' across authors and contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interaction between mathematization and natural philosophy
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate how mathematization transformed disciplines (optics, mechanics, cosmography, cartography) and how mathematical inventions answered natural-philosophical questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use exemplary problems (cartography/integration, optics/perspective, motion/pendulum and cycloid, games of chance/actuarial problems) to show bidirectional influence between mathematics and natural inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nuanced account of mathematics and technology
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid overgeneralizing the role of mathematics in technological change; distinguish areas where practical mathematics influenced technology from fields dominated by craft knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define 'practical mathematics' (knowledge produced by technicians, engineers, artists, merchants) and include both successes (surveying, tables/data, large engineering projects) and failures (unsuccessful mathematization of water-wheel design).

rubrics_metrics.name: Socio-political embedding and state modernization
rubrics_metrics.description: Situate the embedding of mathematical practices within state formation, administrative needs (taxation, centralized data), and modernization processes, especially in the 18th century.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss how states promoted numeracy and education (post-1773 Jesuit suppression as a watershed), recruitment of civil servants, and how mathematical teaching was reorganized to serve administrative aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation and rhetorical strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyse how mathematicians represented and 'sold' their discipline to enhance desirability, prestige, and social status (prints, orations, instruments, title engravings, demonstrations of utility).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine examples of mathematical entrepreneurship (courtly patronage, Jesuit colleges, bookstores), rhetorical devices (promoting utility and epistemic claims), and visual/print strategies that supported status claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professionalization and changing occupational identities
rubrics_metrics.description: Trace the transition from mathematical practitioners to professional mathematicians and the changes in communication, institutionalization, and professional identity across the 18th and 19th centuries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast earlier diverse practitioner roles with later institutional careers; focus on the confluence of social, communicative and organizational changes (wars, administrative reforms) that enabled professionalization.
